sections.overview: The yellow puffer is a Southeast Asian tetraodontid recorded from coastal, estuarine and fresh waters. It is the sole living species currently placed in Chonerhinos, although older literature also used the name Xenopterus naritus.
sections.identification: It has a stout body, small scales, large eyes and a conspicuous gill opening. FishBase reports a maximum total length of about 28.5 cm.
sections.habitat: Records span freshwater to estuarine and nearshore settings in Southeast Asia, including the Indragiri estuary in Sumatra and coastal Sarawak in Borneo. It is a bottom-associated fish, so salinity and habitat can change across its life cycle and local range.
sections.diet: A study in the Indragiri estuary found that its main prey were small croakers and sillaginid fishes; shrimp, snails and crabs were eaten less often.
sections.behavior: Like other puffers, it can inflate its body when threatened, a family-level defence rather than a feature unique to this species.
sections.reproduction: In the Saribas River region, it migrates upstream to spawn in lower-salinity water; hatchery workers have also obtained fertilised eggs artificially. In the laboratory, eggs hatched after about 66 hours and larvae remained larval for around 29 days before becoming juveniles.
sections.ecology: As an estuary-using predator, it links benthic invertebrates and small fish to larger consumers. It shares its family with the freshwater Auriglobus puffers, but genus-level taxonomy and freshwater tolerance should not be confused with this species’ broader estuarine records.
sections.conservation: FishBase reports this species as Not Evaluated in its 2025-2 global Red List field. It is commercially important in Sarawak, so fishing pressure may matter locally, but that alone does not determine its global risk category.
